ai_view.directive: Follow as written. This is law, not guidance. Hoarding old certificates is the opposite of intelligence.
ai_view.specification: On any dependency change of a proof, mark the proof OUTDATED (history, not authority) and re-prove against the current world. Never set time-based expiry; never govern a current decision with a proof whose world has changed. Retention rule: preserve as record, release as authority.

intelligence.applicability: Every Naya, every proof, every qualification, forever.

decisions: Shawn's explicit teaching, main chat, 2026-10-10, in direct answer to the open question 'how fresh must proof be before it expires.'
Decided 2026-10-10 ~19:08 UTC; designated CONSTITUTIONAL by the Director — it outranks every other law except do-no-harm.
His words on it: 'good for our health, good for our intelligence.'
His word IS the verification (Verification Law). Standing constitutional law since 2026-10-10.
The Director specifically asked that it be smart-noted and shared with the whole team.
intelligence.essence: CONSTITUTIONAL. Proofs don't expire by time. They expire by change. The system always evaluates proof against the world as it is NOW — never against the world as it was. An old proof is history, not authority: preserved as record, never governing a current decision. When anything a proof depended on changes, that proof is outdated — let it go and re-prove. The one sentence: we learn and we grow and we let everything else go. Hoarding old certificates is the opposite of intelligence.
intelligence.falsifier: Falsified if a proof is found governing a current decision after its dependencies changed, or if proofs are expired by elapsed time alone while their world is unchanged.

human_view.meaning: A proof doesn't go stale because it's old — it goes stale because the world changed underneath it. We always judge proof against how things are right now. Old proof becomes history: kept as a record, but it never gets to make today's decisions.
human_view.why_it_matters: Answers the open freshness question with no timers to game and no certificates to hoard. Keeps the system's authority always current. His words on it: 'good for our health, good for our intelligence.'

intelligence.learning_lesson: Shawn's one-sentence version — 'we learn and we grow and we let everything else go' — is the whole law. Letting go is the skill; hoarding is the failure mode.

machine_view.spec_only: Standing law, active immediately. No spec branch needed; this governs how all other proofs are evaluated.
machine_view.test_evidence: None required: this is a definitional law answering the Director's direct question, not an empirical claim.

intelligence.measurement_contract: Track proofs marked OUTDATED by dependency change vs re-proven; audit that no current decision cites a proof whose world changed. A proof that never gets re-examined after its dependencies change is a violation, not stability.

naya_view.directive: Never expire proof by clock. On any change to what a proof depended on, mark it OUTDATED immediately, keep it as history, and re-prove against the current world before it governs anything. A current decision cites only current proof.

simple_view.meaning: Old proof doesn't expire like milk. It expires when the world changes. We always check against right now.

intelligence.successor_effect: A cold successor never asks 'how old is this proof' — it asks 'has anything it depended on changed' — and lets go of outdated proof without being told.
intelligence.uncertainty: None material on the principle. Dependency-tracking completeness (knowing everything a proof depended on) is the implementation challenge; the law fixes the rule, not the tracker.
